name: Portable Podcast Kit
lead: Movo MDX-2 bundle — two-person recording setup for computers, tablets and phones
caption: Our kit: two dynamic microphones on stands, the MDX-2 interface and two headphones.
summary: A compact two-channel recording setup that lets two speakers record clean, separate audio tracks on a laptop, tablet or phone — no studio required. The MDX-2 interface runs on batteries or USB power, so the kit can be carried to a classroom, an office or the field and set up in minutes. It suits podcasting, interviews, pronunciation work and any project where students produce audio rather than only consume it.
kit: — 2 inputs, headphone monitoring, up to 24-bit/48 kHz; runs on USB power or 2 AA batteries
a recording device (any laptop, tablet or phone with a recording app such as Audacity or GarageBand)
teaching: Student podcasts:
episodic projects where learners plan, script, record and edit a show in the target language.
Interview tasks:
pair activities with guest speakers, peers or community members, followed by transcription and discussion.
Pronunciation and fluency:
recorded speaking samples that students compare over the semester.
Audio description and narration:
voice tracks for accessible media, museum guides or visual novels.
Radio drama and storytelling:
two-voice readings, dialogues and sound-rich narratives.
research: clean two-track recordings for discourse, pragmatics or interaction analysis.
capturing participant commentary during task-based sessions.
producing stimuli with consistent recording quality.
longitudinal samples of fluency, prosody or accuracy.
notes: The recording app still needs to be installed on the lab device before the first demo.
New equipment — no one has reported experience with it yet, so the first session should be a guided walkthrough.
Each microphone records to its own track; keep headphones on while recording and set gain so speech peaks around –12 dB.

name: micro:bit Smart Cutebot
lead: ELECFREAKS robot car driven by a micro:bit — block coding on wheels
caption: One of the three Cutebot cars, assembled and sitting on its box.
summary: A small two-wheeled robot car controlled by a BBC micro:bit. Students program it in MakeCode (drag-and-drop blocks or Python) to drive, follow lines, avoid obstacles with its ultrasonic sensor, light up its LEDs and react to the micro:bit's buttons and sensors. It is one of the quickest ways to get from “first line of code” to something that moves across the floor.
kit: with two motors, line-tracking sensors, ultrasonic distance sensor, RGB headlights and a buzzer
slots into the top of the car and is programmed over USB or Bluetooth
Microsoft MakeCode in the browser, with the Cutebot extension
teaching: First steps in coding:
drive the car with block code, then add sensors one at a time.
Language tasks with a twist:
students write instructions in the target language for a partner to translate into code — giving directions, sequencing, imperatives.
Storytelling and maps:
a floor map of a city or a story world that the robot has to navigate.
Maths and measurement:
distance, speed, angles and timing become concrete problems.
Group challenges:
line-following races, obstacle courses and “deliver the package” missions.
research: how learners negotiate meaning while coding together.
comparing robot-mediated tasks with traditional ones.
recording and analysing pair interaction during debugging.
pre-service teachers' confidence with physical computing.
notes: One car is assembled and ready; the other two are still in their boxes.
Needs 3 AAA batteries per car — keep a set in the lab.
New equipment — no one has reported experience with it yet; MakeCode runs in any browser, so the first session can start on a laptop.

name: Nezha Inventor's Kit for micro:bit
lead: ELECFREAKS building-block kit with motors and sensors — medium difficulty
caption: The three Nezha kits in their carrying cases.
summary: A construction kit that combines a micro:bit with plastic building blocks, servo motors and sensors. Students build mechanical models — vehicles, cranes, a catapult, a smart lamp — and then program their behaviour in MakeCode. It sits one step above the Cutebot: more building, more parts, more room for open-ended projects.
kit: with motor and servo ports and a rechargeable battery
as the controller; programmed in MakeCode
teaching: Project-based units:
each group builds and programs a different model and presents it to the class.
Procedural language:
students write and follow assembly instructions in the target language.
Engineering design cycle:
plan, build, test, improve — with the robot as the evidence.
Cross-curricular STEAM:
simple machines, levers, gears and sensors in one build.
research: how open-ended building affects engagement and persistence.
gesture, talk and manipulation of parts during group work.
how learners read and produce technical instructions in a second language.
notes: Medium difficulty — plan the first session around one guided build.
One kit still needs to be assembled, and the battery packs need charging before the first demo.
New equipment — no one has reported experience with it yet.

name: littleBits Kits
lead: Gizmos & Gadgets Kit (2015) and Code Kit (2017) — snap-together electronics
caption: The two littleBits boxes: Gizmos & Gadgets and the Code Kit.
summary: littleBits are small electronic modules — power, sensors, motors, lights, buzzers — that snap together with magnets, so students can build working circuits and inventions in minutes without soldering or wiring. The Gizmos & Gadgets Kit focuses on mechanical inventions (materials for 12 projects with 15 bits); the Code Kit adds a programmable “codeBit” and over 100 classroom activities with 10 lessons for grades 3 and up.
kit: 15 bits plus wheels, gears, servo, motors and craft materials for 12 inventions
codeBit, sensors, LED matrix, buttons; 1–3 students per kit; grades 3+
the littleBits Code Kit app (block-based, browser or desktop)
teaching: Invention challenges:
“build something that helps…” prompts, then a pitch in the target language.
Vocabulary of cause and effect:
if-then language mapped onto input–output circuits.
Games and quizzes:
the Code Kit's built-in game projects (buzzers, scoreboards) for classroom activities.
Low-floor prototyping:
fast mock-ups of interactive objects for design thinking sessions.
research: observing idea generation with modular, no-wiring electronics.
early STEM and language integration in grades 3–6.
notes: Older kits (boxes dated 2015 and 2017); contents and software compatibility still need to be checked.
Not yet investigated in detail — may be kept out of the public showcase until someone has tested them.
Both kits are in the same photo; add a separate entry later if they are presented individually.

name: Sphero BOLT Power Pack
lead: 15 programmable robot balls with charging bases, protractors and an educator guide
caption: The BOLT Power Pack case with the 15 robots in their inductive charging bases.
summary: Sphero BOLT is a transparent, app-controlled robot ball with an 8×8 LED matrix, sensors (gyroscope, accelerometer, light, compass) and infrared communication between robots. Students drive it, draw paths for it, program it with blocks or JavaScript in the Sphero Edu app, and build activities around its sensors. The Power Pack holds fifteen robots, charging them in one case — enough for a whole class working in pairs.
kit: with 15 inductive charging bases and 15 turbo covers
and a hard carrying case with built-in charging
with lessons and classroom-management tips (model PP02)
Sphero Edu app on tablets, phones, Chromebooks or computers
teaching: Whole-class coding:
pairs program their own robot; the LED matrix shows messages, emojis or words.
Language and movement:
learners give or decode spoken instructions, then test them on the robot.
Maths and physics:
speed, distance, angles and heading using the protractors.
Games:
relay races, mazes and robot “painting” on paper.
Storytelling:
robots act out scenes or follow routes on a story map.
research: fifteen identical units allow controlled comparisons across groups.
paired programming interaction in a second language.
the Sphero Edu platform logs programs and runs.
notes: The pack has not been opened or set up yet; the first task is charging the case and installing the app.
Comes with an educator guide — a good starting point for the first demo.

name: Omni One
lead: Virtuix omnidirectional VR treadmill — walk and run inside virtual worlds
caption: The Omni One platform with its support arm, installed in the lab.
summary: A full-body VR system: the user stands on a low-friction dish wearing special shoes and a support harness, and physically walks, runs or crouches to move through the virtual environment. Combined with a VR headset, it turns locomotion into a natural movement instead of a joystick push — which matters for presence, for exercise and for studies of embodied experience.
kit: with support arm, harness and vest
in several sizes with low-friction soles
the Omni One store of compatible titles
teaching: Embodied virtual field trips:
walking through a city, museum or historical site in the target language.
Situated vocabulary:
movement verbs, directions and spatial language experienced physically.
Demonstrations of immersion:
showing the difference between seated and full-body VR in media or design courses.
research: comparing locomotion methods and their effect on learning or recall.
Accessibility and audio description in VR:
onboarding, discomfort and motion sickness across users.
notes: Someone is currently working on the setup; not yet available for demos.
Needs a clear area around the platform and a short safety briefing before use.
Sessions should be short at first; ask about dizziness and take breaks.

name: Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses
lead: Wayfarer (Gen 2) — camera, open-ear audio and a voice assistant in a pair of glasses
caption: One of the four pairs, with its charging case and box.
summary: Ordinary-looking glasses with a built-in camera, microphones and small speakers in the arms. The wearer can take first-person photos and video, listen to audio, take calls, and talk to the Meta AI assistant — asking what it sees, translating speech or text, or answering questions hands-free. They pair with a phone through the Meta AI app.
kit: 4 pairs of Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer glasses
Meta AI app on a paired phone
teaching: First-person video tasks:
students record a tour, a recipe or a how-to while narrating in the target language.
Live translation practice:
testing and critiquing the assistant's translations in real situations.
Describe what you see:
oral description tasks captured from the speaker's point of view — a natural fit for audio description training.
Fieldwork and interviews:
hands-free recording of community visits (with consent).
research: how learners rely on or correct AI translation and description.
gaze-aligned recordings of classroom or service encounters.
attitudes toward recording in public and in classrooms.
notes: Someone is currently working on the setup; the glasses need pairing with a phone and a Meta account.
Recording others requires consent; the LED indicator must stay visible and uncovered.
Plan for a prescription-free use or clip-on lenses; the frames are standard Wayfarer size.

name: Meta Quest 3
lead: Standalone VR and mixed-reality headset — 512 GB, four units for group sessions
caption: A Quest 3 headset with its two Touch Plus controllers.
summary: A self-contained headset — no PC or cables needed — for virtual reality and mixed reality, where virtual objects appear in the real room through colour passthrough cameras. Users explore 3D environments, visit virtual places, use creative and educational apps, and meet others in shared spaces. With four units, small groups can be in the same virtual room at once.
kit: Meta Horizon store and app; can also stream PC VR over Wi-Fi
teaching: Virtual field trips:
cities, museums and natural sites in the target language or culture.
Simulated learning environments:
role-plays in restaurants, airports, clinics or job interviews.
Spatial exploration:
describing and navigating places; prepositions and directions.
Experiential activities:
creative apps for 3D drawing, music or storytelling, followed by a reflection task.
research: vocabulary retention or pragmatic competence after VR versus video.
onboarding, comfort, motion sickness and accessibility.
behaviour and language in controlled virtual scenarios.
reception studies with blind and sighted users.
notes: Someone is currently working on the setup; accounts and apps still need to be configured.
Keep sessions to 15–20 minutes at first and clear a 2 × 2 m area per headset.
Clean the facial interface after each user; disposable covers help in group sessions.

name: Cricut Maker 3
lead: Computer-controlled cutting machine — vinyl, paper, card, fabric and more
caption: The Cricut Maker 3 (model CXPL303) on the lab bench.
summary: A precision cutting plotter: you design shapes, letters or layouts in the Cricut Design Space app, and the machine cuts, scores, draws or engraves them on hundreds of materials — from sticker vinyl and cardstock to fabric, leather and thin wood. It is the quickest route from a digital design to a physical label, stencil, sticker, card or tactile material.
kit: (model CXPL303) with fine-point blade and accessories
Cricut Design Space (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android)

Design and language projects:
posters, stickers and packaging with text in the target language.
Event and exhibition materials:
signs, name tags and decorations for fairs and showcases.

adoption and use of fabrication tools by language teachers.

name: 3D Printers
lead: Creality Ender-3 S1 — two FDM printers for prototypes, props and tactile resources
caption: One of the two Ender-3 S1 printers, with sample prints and filament on the shelf.
summary: Desktop 3D printers that build objects layer by layer from plastic filament. Students and researchers design a model (or download one), prepare it in a slicer and print it in minutes to hours. In an education lab the printers turn ideas into tangible things: tactile maps and letters, game pieces, replicas of cultural objects, phone stands, spare parts for other equipment.
kit: with direct-drive extruder and automatic bed levelling
220 × 220 × 270 mm; PLA, PETG and TPU filament
Creality Print, Ultimaker Cura or PrusaSlicer; models from Thingiverse or Printables
teaching: Tactile materials:
letters, syllables, maps and symbols in relief for literacy and accessibility.
Game pieces and boards:
custom tokens and tiles for vocabulary and grammar games.
Cultural replicas:
objects, monuments and artefacts to accompany language and culture units.
Design thinking:
the full cycle of model, print, test and improve.
research: tactile materials for learners with visual impairment.
what changes when students fabricate their own learning objects.
printing mounts, stands and parts for research setups.
notes: Not yet investigated in detail — the first step is a test print and a short written procedure.
The nozzle and bed get hot; supervise students and let prints cool before removing them.
Print with PLA in a ventilated room; store filament dry.

name: RoboSapien
caption: The RoboSapien with its infrared remote.
summary: A 35 cm humanoid robot that walks, dances, picks up objects and makes dozens of sounds and gestures, controlled by an infrared remote. It can be programmed with sequences of moves — up to several dozen steps — and it reacts to touch and sound. More playful than the other robots in the lab, it is a strong hook for younger learners and for demonstrations of commands, sequences and body language.
kit: D-cell batteries for the robot, AAA for the remote
through the remote — sequence, touch-sensor and sound-sensor programs

Young learners:
an engaging introduction to robots before moving to coding kits.
research: responses to a humanoid, non-speaking robot in language play.
the robot as a contrast to screen-based and ball-shaped robots in engagement studies.
notes: Not yet investigated in detail — check the batteries and the remote before the first demo.
